asgRatings.title: Ongoing Assessment for Wytham House
asgRatings.name: Care Homes
asgRatings.commentary:
Date of Assessment: 20 May to 5 June 2025. Wytham House is a care home providing personal and nursing care to people aged 65 and over living with dementia. The care home accommodates up to 40 people across three separate units laid over two floors. On the day of our inspection 32 people were living at the home. This was an unannounced, responsive assessment, prompted by emerging risk.

We found breaches of regulation in relation to safe care and treatment and good governance.

The home worked with a number of professionals to ensure continuity of care within the home. Lessons were learnt to identify and embed good practice. Staff knew people and their risks well. However, care records contained conflicting information, and did not always document support required to keep people safe. Assessments were not always in place or person-centred.

The home was clean and incorporated a dementia friendly environment.

Dependency tools were used to calculate the correct number of staff. However, clinical tools such as risk assessments did not always accurately reflect people’s needs, which could impact the number of staff required. We heard from staff there were times where more staff were needed to support people and their needs.

Staff felt supported by leaders who provided support. Staff received relevant training and demonstrated a good understanding of people and their needs in relation to dementia care. Information around people’s ability to consent was not well documented.

Medicines were well managed. However, documentation was not always reflective of people’s needs around medicines.

The home raised safeguarding appropriately however we found instances where people were put at risk of harm due to poor moving and handling techniques.

There were meal choices at lunch time and people were shown alternatives before making their selections.

The governance systems in place had not identified and addressed the concerns found during inspection. Audits did not always capture incidents which allowed the home to act on information of concern. Actions were not always reflective of documentation in place.

In instances where CQC have decided to take civil or criminal enforcement action against a provider, we will publish this information on our website after any representations and/ or appeals have been concluded.
asgRatings.narrative: The service is performing well and meeting our expectations.
asgRatings.overallPeopleExperience:
People were cared for in a safe environment which was designed to meet their needs, and people were encouraged and supported to raise concerns

Although not always involved in care planning, people using the service and their relatives told us they felt safe and were happy with their care. People told us, “I think the care is good here, I think anyone would always prefer there to be more carers, but I think the numbers here cover adequately.”

Some people could not directly tell us about their experience. We therefore also observed people being supported throughout the day of the visit to assess whether they received good care. We observed staff were caring however, some practices which did not always consider the person.

We received good feedback about the food at the home, and positive feedback about the service being proactive about people’s clinical needs.

keyQuestionRatings.name: Effective
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Effective – this means we looked for evidence that people’s care, treatment and support achieved good outcomes and promoted a good quality of life, based on best available evidence.

At our last assessment we rated this key question good. At this assessment the rating has remained good. This meant people’s outcomes were consistently good, and people’s feedback confirmed this.

topicareas.name: Assessing needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had systems in place to assess people’s needs, however, they were not robust and did not always ensure care plans and risk assessments were updated regularly.

Although there were care plans and some risk assessments in place, they were not fully reflective of people’s needs. For example, risk assessments were not always reflective of people’s mobility needs, they did not provide guidance on what support was needed with people’s mobility or what equipment they used. Assessments did not always cover the risk to oral care, pressure care concerns, medical diagnosis, or behaviours. Information about people’s needs was not always consistent throughout care plans. This meant staff did not have enough information to support the person safely.

Staff knew people and their needs well, they were updated within changes to people’s care needs explained how they would seek support from external services where people’s needs changed.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Consent to care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider respected people’s rights when delivering care and treatment. However, information about people’s capacity was not always consistent within people’s care planning documentation and did not always evidence who had Lasting Power of Attorney, or how decisions had been made. However, there was a clear understanding of the Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards (DoLS) and this was only used when it is in the best interest of the person.

There were some practices seen on the day where language around supporting people, did not always consider the person, however, staff we spoke with understood the importance of obtaining consent before they delivered care or treatment.

Staff provided examples of how they would support people with dementia and demonstrated empathy and understanding. Staff told us, “I give people lots of different questions to people who are non-verbal, for example, until we get it right. You need to be proactive and responsive to anticipate people’s needs. We know people well. I always try to put myself in the person’s position, I use patience to understand people, although they may not be able to communicate effectively, they can listen, I always apply empathy.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Delivering evidence-based care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider planned and delivered people’s care and treatment with them, including what was important and mattered to them. They did this in line with legislation and current evidence-based good practice and standards.

There were meal choices at lunch time and people were shown alternatives before making their selections. One relative told us, “The food is so much better, and [person] gets the correct food here.”

During the inspection we observed limited drinks being offered throughout the day. Some care plans contained details about people’s likes and dislikes around foods with good information about how to support them.

People were referred to appropriate services when required. Nationally recognised tools were used to ensure people were supported correctly with their eating and drinking needs. The chef was experienced and demonstrated a passion and a good knowledge of the people’s dietary needs as well as their likes and dislikes.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: How staff, teams and services work together

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider worked well across teams and services to support people. There were processes in place to ensure staff worked well together.

Relatives told us they were kept updated about their loved ones changing health needs.

The home carried out team meetings, handovers were being carried out and the provider worked closely with external health professionals.

Although some staff told us about workload being difficult with staffing at time, we heard the team worked well together. Staff told us, “We have seniors who support on many occasions” and “Carers listen and respond positively, my colleagues are very supportive.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Monitoring and improving outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always routinely monitor people’s care and treatment to continuously improve it. The service did not ensure people’s care plans were updated to reflect changes in their care needs. This made it difficult to monitor outcomes.

People’s care was monitored weekly within clinical meetings to ensure there was oversight of people’s clinical needs. There was limited detail documented about action required, or who was responsible for the action, in order to direct staff to ensure positive outcomes were achieved. Clinical audits did not always capture incidents, and did not always pick up on missing actions. This meant there were some cases where incidents were not always investigated in a timely manner.

There were good wound plans in place and staff were aware of peoples changing needs.

Relatives we spoke with felt they had not had to raise concerns about safety or incidents and reported positive outcomes since moving to the home. One relative told us how staff were proactive at ensuring their loved one was seen quickly when unwell. We also heard, “We are so pleased that the GP here is the one we knew before- everything is so much better here [person] is physically much better now.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Supporting people to live healthier lives

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider supported people to manage their health and wellbeing to maximise their independence, choice, and control. Staff supported people to live healthier lives and where possible, reduce their future needs for care and support.

People were supported to access health care professionals when they needed them and received ongoing care from healthcare professionals. There was a regular GP round, and professionals told us staff were organised and proactive.

Physical activities were carried out by the service, we heard from one relative, “I came and enjoyed the athletics yesterday, I saw that all the staff enjoyed themselves and most of the residents loved it too.”

keyQuestionRatings.name: Safe
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Safe – this means we looked for evidence that people were protected from abuse and avoidable harm. At our last assessment we rated this key question good. At this assessment the rating has changed to requires improvement. This meant some aspects of the service were not always safe and there was limited assurance about safety. There was an increased risk that people could be harmed.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to people’s safe care and treatment and governance at the service.

topicareas.name: Infection prevention and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider assessed and managed the risk of infection. They detected and controlled the risk of it spreading and shared concerns with appropriate agencies promptly.

The home presented as clean and had regular cleaning protocols in place. Communal areas and people’s rooms appeared to be clean, clear of obstruction and rubbish.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Involving people to manage risks

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always work well with people to understand and manage risks. Staff did not always provide care to meet people’s needs that was safe, supportive and enabled people to do the things that mattered to them.

Risk assessments about care and people’s support needs were not always assessed or person-centred. For example, there was missing and or contradictory information about people’s physical ability, communication, level of support required, repositioning and equipment used. Care plans were reviewed monthly, however information was not always updated within the care plan to evidence people’s changes in needs. The provider told us they would review their care planning process following the inspection.

During the onsite inspection, we observed incidents when care staff did not always respond to people’s distress. There were limited assessments or guidance which would enable staff to support people when they were distressed.

People who used the service and their relatives were not always involved in their care planning. This was something which had already been identified by the provider as needing to be introduced, however, we heard people felt safe and happy with their care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had a proactive and positive culture of safety, based on openness and honesty. Staff listened to concerns about safety and investigated and reported safety events. Lessons were learnt to identify and embed good practice.

People and staff were encouraged and supported to raise concerns, they felt confident they would be treated with compassion and understanding.

Staff told us they were updated about incidents and changes. Incidents and accidents were discussed in handovers, meetings and group supervisions.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Medicines optimisation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always make sure medicines and treatments were safe and met people’s needs, capacities, and preferences. Staff involved people in planning, including when changes happened. The service contacted the GP regularly regarding changes with medicines.

Medicines were well managed. Staff were knowledgeable about medicines and people's behaviour was not inappropriately controlled by medicines. There were appropriate arrangements for the safe management, use and oversight of drugs. However, care plans did not detail where creams were to be applied and had not been updated to reflect changes to people’s medicines.

One person’s care planning documentation stated they were compliant with their medicines, however, these medicines were given to them covertly. For another person who was receiving their medicines covertly, there was no information within the care plan regarding how these were administered.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider made sure staff were qualified, skilled and experienced, who received effective support, supervision and development. However, we heard additional staff on an evening would ensure more effective support, care notes we reviewed for one person documented they had to wait for support with personal care.

People told us, “I think the care is good here, I think anyone would always prefer there to be more carers, but I think the numbers here cover adequately.” Relatives we spoke with considered staff numbers could be higher, however, did not feel staff levels impacted on their loved one’s care.

We observed agency staff did not always know people's names. On some occasions we observed limited engagement staff to people using the service, however staff did not appear rushed and often spoke to people with kindness

Staff provided mixed feedback around staffing levels and had raised concerns with the service about staffing levels; although changes had been made to shift patterns, there has been no changes to staffing levels following this. Staff told us, “I am frustrated if there are not enough staff, we only have three and a half over these two Units and one other until 3pm and if someone is sick it is very difficult”, but this did not happen too often.

Staff receive training appropriate and relevant to their role and felt supported to deliver care. The service carried out supervisions. Staff felt they had enough training and training was ongoing. There were robust and safe recruitment practices in place.

The provider told us they used dependency tools to ensure the correct number of staff were on shift.However, assessments in place did not always accurately reflect people’s needs, which could impact the number of staff required to deliver safe care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe environments

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider detected and controlled potential risks in the care environment. They made sure equipment, facilities and technology supported the delivery of safe care.

People were cared for in a safe environment which was designed to meet their needs. The home has been specifically designed to incorporate a dementia friendly environment. The corridors and communal rooms were spacious and clean.

We heard good examples from staff about how they would keep people safe in relation to the environment. Leaders and staff considered how environments can keep people safe from psychological harm as well as physical harm.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe systems, pathways and transitions

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider worked with people and healthcare partners to establish and maintain safe systems of care, in which safety was managed or monitored. However, people’s information was not always up to date to ensure professions had enough detail if people moved between services.

The home worked with a number of professionals to ensure continuity of care within the home. The home had regular visits from the GP and made appropriate referrals to healthcare professionals.

Staff knew people and their risks well and told us how they worked with professionals to keep people safe. Despite awareness of risks to people and positive feedback, care records contained conflicting information, and did not always document support to mitigate risk, which could impact the way services work together to ensure safe transitions between services.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safeguarding

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider worked with people and healthcare partners to understand what being safe meant to them and the best way to achieve that. The provider shared concerns quickly and appropriately with the safeguarding team. There was one occurrence where the police had not been contacted following an incident, the provider acted appropriately by notifying the CQC, raising a safeguarding alert, dismissed the staff member and made a DBS referral, however they failed to notify police on this 1 occasion.

The home raised safeguarding appropriately and arranged meetings with professionals to discuss concerns. Notifications were submitted to the Commission to notify us of incidents. However, during the inspection we observed 2 incidents where people were put at risk of harm due to poor moving and handling techniques.

Care plans and risk assessments did not provide guidance which would allow staff to understand how to support people with safe moving and handling techniques. We told the provider about these concerns, and were assured the correct guidance would be put in place to ensure safe practices were carried out.

People using the service and their relatives told us they felt safe and were happy with their care. We were told, “I have lived here for some time, I like it, everyone is always very helpful towards me” and “Yes, [person] is absolutely safe here, they look after [person] so well.”

Staff we spoke to knew people and their needs well, had access to safeguarding policies, received safeguarding training, and further guidance was available within their staff handbook.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Well-led – this means we looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation; and promoted an open, fair culture.

At our last assessment we rated this key question good. At this assessment the rating has changed to requires improvement. This meant the management and leadership was inconsistent. Leaders and the culture they created did not always support the delivery of high-quality, person-centred care.

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had inclusive leaders at all levels who understood the context in which they delivered care, treatment and support and embodied the culture and values of their workforce and organisation. Leaders had the skills, knowledge, experience and credibility to lead effectively. They did so with integrity, openness and honesty.

Staff felt safe and supported by leaders, who were visible and led by example. We heard, “I have direct access to my manager, and I can ask anything I want” and “Managers have come to the floor to assist me which is strange with as from my previous experience I have not had this support before. I can talk to [the manager] where I think I think I might need encouragement. [The manager] has given me ideas, and we work as a team.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider fostered a positive culture where people felt they could speak up and their voice would be heard.

Staff knew who to approach if they needed to speak up and told us they felt respected, and Wytham was a positive place to work.

Processes in place provided staff with opportunity to speak up if they had any concerns. Staff were aware of who they would speak to if they had any concerns around culture and practice at the service.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had clear responsibilities, roles, systems of accountability and good governance systems in place. However, governance systems were not always utilised to identify concerns found during the inspection.

Leaders told us risks were analysed in the monthly clinical governance meetings. Following the inspection, we received a clinical governance meeting minute document. Although the meeting documented action taken, there was not always a target date, or person responsible for ensuring the actions were complete. We found that clinical meetings and clinical audits identified concerns around pressure sores and bruising. Information had not always updated within peoples care planning or risk assessments. Clinical meetings and audits did not contain all incidents that had taken place, or document the action taken to mitigate the risk.

Some systems and processes required further development, for example, the auditing of care plans. Care planning audits had not always followed up on required improvements as they did not contain all actions or identify information had not been updated to reflect the persons current needs. The provider told us they would take immediate action to review their current systems and documentation in place following the inspection.

Audits of the service were completed regularly. Audits which required a scoring, did not always accurately reflect the score when reviewing the comments within the audit, and there were no additional comments or actions documented in order for the service to follow up on.Some actions from audits were not identified on the service improvement plan in order to ensure improvements could be made. The previous improvement plan contained completed actions, however, we found information in peoples care planning was not accurate despite being documented as achieved.

Data and notifications were consistently submitted to external organisations as required.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider focused on continuous learning, innovation and improvement across the organisation and local system. They encouraged creative ways of delivering equality of experience, outcome and quality of life for people. They actively contributed to safe, effective practice and research. There were processes to ensure learning happened when things go wrong. Leaders encourage reflection and collective problem-solving.

There were processes in place for learning and improvement. Investigating incidents was not always carried out in a timely manner to ensure learning was implemented, however, where these had been carried out, there were good examples of lessons learnt following some concerns found in audits.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider understood their duty to collaborate and work in partnership, so services worked seamlessly for people. They shared information and learning with partners and collaborated for improvement.

Staff and leaders were open and transparent, and they collaborated with relevant external stakeholders and agencies. We heard positive feedback from professionals about how the service updated them about outcomes from safeguarding or actions they had taken to keep people safe.

Professionals told us there had been recent improvements to the service around risk, the service was more protective in how they responded to and managed risk. Staff were knowledgeable and the service is forthcoming and organised. how communication had improved over the last several months.

Staff and leaders work in partnership with key organisations to support care provision.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had a shared vision, strategy and culture. This was based on transparency, equity, equality and human rights, diversity and inclusion, engagement, and understanding challenges and the needs of people and their communities.

Staff and leaders demonstrated a positive, compassionate, listening culture which promoted trust and understanding between them and people using the service.

There was a shared direction and culture, staff, professionals and people/relatives all commented on positive changes over the last several months.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider valued diversity in their workforce. They worked towards an inclusive and fair culture by improving equality and equity for people who worked for them. Staff had completed training in equality and diversity.

Staff told us they felt supported in their role, if they had any concerns they would be acted on. We observed a positive culture during our onsite inspection. New staff were made to feel welcome at the workplace.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care
